title: 🥊 Retailers beat the bad vibes
body_text: A slew of states have now enacted cell phone bans in schools, which keep phones, watches and connected tablets locked away from bell-to-bell. Some of the immediate benefits, like encouraging students to, uhhh, talk to each other, are obvious. Harvard researchers, however, took things a step further. They looked at students in 4,600 schools across the US and found that school cell phone bans helped students learn more. They found that in schools where phones and other devices were kept locked away during the day, students gained the academic equivalent of one to two additional weeks of instruction per year, the Wall Street Journal reported . “Pretty soon we’ll look back and think it’s crazy that students could use their phones whenever they want to,” Thomas Kane, an author of the study and director of the Harvard Center for Education Policy Research, told the WSJ. Earlier this week I wrote that American consumers feeling increasingly pessimistic about the cost of living was increasingly not Walmart ’s problem. Case in point: The retail giant reported earnings results that narrowly beat Wall Street estimates and raised its full-year sales and earnings outlook. Its US e-commerce sales jumped 23%, even as comparable sales growth slowed from a year earlier. Target , another place that sells both staples and cheap knickknacks, crushed quarterly estimates and hiked its guidance after posting its best sales growth in five years. TJX , which owns discount retailers TJ Maxx and Marshalls, also beat estimates. These retailers describe catering to a value-conscious customer. “Busy families are watching their budgets and being thoughtful about where they spend, and we see them responding when we give them something they love at a price that feels right,” Cara Sylvester, chief merchandising officer at Target, told analysts. US retail sales slowed in October as purchases of big-ticket items like cars and furniture slipped, according to the most recent reading from the Commerce Department released Tuesday. That checks out with what both Home Depot and Lowe’s reported: smaller repair and maintenance projects helped drive their sales beats, even as larger discretionary renovations remained under pressure. Both face macroeconomic headwinds, like high borrowing costs and a slow housing market. “Well, Simeon, housing turnover hasn't moved in four years now,” Richard McPhail, Home Depot’s current CFO and incoming CEO, quipped at a Morgan Stanley analyst. He attributed several positive quarters to market share gains. “Our investments are designed to position us to capture share regardless of the economic environment,” he said. Retailers seem to be successfully adapting to a world where people are pinching pennies and feel like life is ripping them off. Target is cutting prices, TJ Maxx is trying to attract bargain hunters across income brackets, and Home Depot is catering to homeowners who would rather fix up their current place than trade their cheap mortgage for a much more expensive one. The industry appears to be well poised for a strong holiday shopping season. For now, retailers seem to have figured out how to keep Americans spending even when they don't feel particularly good about it. title: 👍 Nvidia will probably be fine
body_text: Americans are in love with fried chicken, but that fervor has largely sidestepped KFC. The Yum Brands chain’s US sales keep falling and the pain is hitting franchises: a major franchisee is filing for bankruptcy, according to court filings . Tasty Chick’n LLC operates 75 KFCs and 9 Taco Bells across 10 Southeastern and Midwestern states and owes Yum more than $15 million in unpaid royalties. (Franchisees operate as independent businesses but must pay portions of their sales to the franchisor.) Franchise agreements can require remodelling and other upgrades to locations and that appears to be the root of the unpaid royalties in this case – another reminder that when big, national fast food chains embark on turnarounds, there’s often a bevy of regional operators footing most of the bill. In one of the most anticipated quarterly earnings reports in years, on Tuesday Nvidia bested Wall Street’s expectations for earnings and revenue and posted guidance ahead of analysts’ estimates. So that means the Jensen Huang saga is firmly behind the chip behemoth, right? Right? Insert Padme meme here . A bevy of Silicon Valley bigwigs are now calling for Huang’s reinstatement. Nevermind the looming Capital Hill hearings , the only-just-begun internal corporate investigations into who knew what, and whatever the federal law enforcement agencies and securities regulators might choose to do, Elon Musk and a bevy of venture capitalists think Huang and only Huang can be an effective CEO of Nvidia. For his part, Huang has been listening, learning, and reflecting. And, in a statement released five days after he tendered his resignation, he’s decided that he’s open to returning as CEO of the company he co-founded. (The board says it has ruled out his return and has reached out to Arm Holdings Plc Chief Executive Officer Rene Haas, Bloomberg News reported Wednesday.) The stock has taken a beating in recent months. As Entrypoint’s Luke Kawa pointed out, the company is paradoxically in an extremely strong position , and investors could stand to benefit thanks to both the (relatively) beaten down shares and the continued demand for AI chips. “Demand did not resign,” was the quip from Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives. In Kawa’s estimation, interim CEO Colette Kress “her hands are on the wheel of a profit powerhouse that’s on cruise control thanks to the prior navigator.” They say one sign of an effective manager is if the organization they run can operate effectively without them. It’s understandable that many executives would rather not find out if they’ve achieved that kind of success, but Huang very well may have. The road back – at least, at Nvidia – looks very much like a dead-end at the moment. Things might be different if Nvidia’s biggest customers were jumping ship. But they’re not really doing that. Amazon ’s Jeff Bezos declined to say whether Huang should be reinstated, saying he lacked enough information to voice an opinion. OpenAI’s Sam Altman – who knows a bit about being ousted and reinstated at the helm of an organization he helped create – expressed “extreme, extreme gratitude” for Huang taking an early bet on OpenAI, and said it’s “hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen.” But as Huang surely recognizes, that’s not exactly a clarion call for his return. That’s particularly indicative of the slim chances Huang has for a reinstatement, given Altman is arguably the AI exec most plugged into the network of Bay Area venture capitalists who have been most strident in their support for the ex-Nvidia CEO’s return. title: 🛒 Retail vibe check
body_text: It is a modern age of miracles with the dawn of AI, and if you’re going to succeed at a time like this you’ve got to be willing to turn your business model around on a dime and deliver what the people want. Take a buzzy startup called Inception AI that used LLMs to generate 15,000 AI-generated podcasts hosted by more than 50 AI personalities to produce some 3,000 episodes a week for $1 an episode or less. The startup has cracked a brilliant, innovative, and daring new business model: just hiring human hosts . Turns out audiences liked them way more, and nobody was particularly interested in what quickly became 350,000 episodes of digital chum. Who could have thought? Stocks fell on Tuesday. After the bell, Nvidia beat on both top and bottom lines . Investors are getting a vibe check from American consumers this week, with the first big slew of data arriving after the US midterm elections, where concerns over the cost of living took center stage. Here’s a summary of some of the data Wall Street has to mull this week: US retail sales slowed in October as purchases of big ticket items like cars and furniture slipped, according to the most recent reading from the Commerce Department released Tuesday. Home improvement giant Home Depot reported sales and profit numbers that beat expectations but narrowed its profit guidance, setting the stage for its competitor Lowe’s to report on Wednesday. Both companies also face pressure from high mortgage rates. In an environment where it is harder to purchase a home, there is less reason for trips to their stores. Target will also report on Wednesday, as will TJX , the company behind the discount retailer TJ Maxx. Finally, on Thursday we get the big one: Walmart . What these companies report and what they say on their earnings calls will give investors a sense of how they are positioned going into the holiday season. And to put a bow on it, the University of Michigan’s latest Consumer Sentiment Index reading lands on Friday. The index has been hovering around historic lows this year. This data comes as a relatively resilient labor market and a stock market that, until recently, had been climbing helped keep consumers spending, particularly wealthier Americans who own stocks and other assets. Consumers are keeping the US economy chugging along, but not with a smile on their faces. Americans have been increasingly unhappy watching the price of gas and other goods go up and up while Silicon Valley types get richer and richer. And that’s increasingly not Walmart’s problem. For the past several years there’s been a growing disconnect between how much consumers are spending and their attitudes about the economy. They are still purchasing discretionary items like “Grand Theft Auto VI” while feeling pessimistic about their finances. That’s largely because employment has stayed steady. Smaller luxuries like a new videogame or a modest home renovation project are still in the budget, but buying a home, or even a car or new couch, is not. After this week investors will have a clearer picture on whether consumers are pulling back or simply getting pickier.
